subject: general
question: Why does growth in plants occur only in specific regions?

options.text: Water reaches only the upper parts of the plant.
Gravity prevents growth in certain regions.
Only some parts of the plant receive sunlight.
Meristematic tissue is located only in specific regions.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Meristematic tissue is located only in specific regions.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• Plant growth occurs in specific regions because of the presence of **meristematic tissue**. These tissues are undifferentiated and actively divide to contribute to the growth of the plant.
 
• **Meristematic tissues** are located in certain areas such as the tips of roots and shoots (apical meristems), the circumference of stems and roots (lateral meristems), and certain areas of leaves (intercalary meristems).
 
• The cells in the meristematic tissue are small, thin-walled, with a dense cytoplasm and large nuclei, making them capable of continuous division.
 
• Unlike other plant tissues, meristematic tissues do not specialize or mature into permanent tissue, ensuring continuous growth in specific regions.
 
• Other parts of the plant, such as mature leaves or stems, do not grow because they contain **permanent tissues**, which are specialized and incapable of division.
